extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court Justices and clerks; appellate patent counsel
extracted.subtask_description: A brief in opposition to a petition for writ of certiorari arguing that the Federal Circuit’s use of the ensnarement defense (a limitation on the doctrine of equivalents) is longstanding, non-controversial, was waived below, and does not violate the Seventh Amendment. It addresses substantive patent-law standards and procedural rules governing appellate review and jury/bench allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement vs. doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine literal infringement, the accused device is compared against the elements of the patent claim: if the device includes every requirement of the claim, it literally infringes. If it does not literally infringe, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if a component of the accused device that does not literally meet the corresponding requirement 'performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result.' Graver Tank & Mfg. Co. v. Linde Air Prods. Co., 339 U.S. 605.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Graver Tank function-way-result test to assess whether non-literal components nonetheless infringe under equivalents; first attempt literal comparison element-by-element, then apply equivalents test only where literal infringement fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art circumscribes doctrine of equivalents (ensnarement principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: An important limitation on the doctrine of equivalents is that it is always circumscribed by the prior art: if the aspect alleged to infringe under equivalents would not have been patentable at the time the patent was sought because it would also cover the prior art, it cannot form the basis for a judgment of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. (Wilson Sporting Goods Co. v. David Geoffrey & Assocs., 904 F.2d 677).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the doctrine of equivalents, evaluate the scope of prior art contemporaneous with the patent application; deny equivalents-based infringement if the asserted equivalent would have anticipated or rendered unpatentable a hypothetical claim of that breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent may not 'ensnare' the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A patent may not, through the doctrine of equivalents, unduly invade or "ensnare" the prior art.' (Wilson Sporting Goods, 904 F.2d at 685).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'ensnarement' as the label for the court's role in preventing a patentee from using equivalents to obtain protection that would improperly appropriate subject matter in the prior art; if an equivalent would 'ensnare' prior art, reject the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff bears burden to show a patentable equivalent (no burden-shifting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the plaintiff bears the burden of proving patent infringement, 'the burden of showing that there could exist a patentable equivalent to a claim also falls on the plaintiff.' Wilson Sporting Goods, 904 F.2d at 684.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require the patentee/plaintiff to demonstrate that a hypothetical claim broadened to cover the accused device would have been patentable (i.e., would not have been anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art); do not treat this as shifting the defendant's burden to prove invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical claim used to test ensnarement must be properly broadened and patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: In the district court, the patentee submitted hypothetical claims expanded to cover the accused device; the court concluded that neither hypothetical claim was proper 'because neither had been broadened in scope,' and therefore vacated the jury verdict of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When courts require a hypothetical claim for ensnarement analysis, the hypothetical must be a properly broadened claim that would literally encompass the accused product; the court then assesses whether that broadened claim would have been patentable over the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensnarement and prosecution-history estoppel are legal limitations resolved by judge
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensnarement is, like prosecution-history estoppel, a legal limitation on the doctrine of equivalents and therefore is resolved as a question of law by the judge rather than as a jury fact issue. Warner-Jenkinson Co. v. Hilton Davis Chem. Co., 520 U.S. 17; DePuy Spine, Inc. v. Medtronic Sofamor Danek, Inc., 567 F.3d 1314.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate ensnarement/resolution of patentable-hypothetical questions to the court; courts may set aside jury verdicts on equivalents grounds when legal limitations (ensnarement/prosecution-history estoppel) preclude a verdict of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Amendment waiver and preservation rules for appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: This Court traditionally denies certiorari 'when the question presented was not pressed or passed upon below.' United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36. The petitioner never challenged the constitutionality of the ensnarement defense below; therefore the Federal Circuit did not pass upon the question and it is waived for certiorari review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Supreme Court review of a constitutional argument, ensure the issue was adequately raised and passed upon in lower courts; new constitutional issues not presented below are presumptively inappropriate for certiorari absent exceptional circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-trial JMOLs and bench resolution of legal issues do not violate the Seventh Amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-trial hearings to resolve dispositive questions of law (e.g., ensnarement) comport with the Seventh Amendment; courts routinely set aside jury verdicts on renewed JMOLs. The Reexamination Clause does not prevent a court from reexamining legal questions after a verdict. Baltimore & Carolina Line v. Redman, 295 U.S. 654; Neely v. Martin K. Eby Const. Co., Inc., 386 U.S. 317.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may reserve legal questions for post-verdict hearings or enter renewed JMOLs that resolve legal limitations on verdicts; preservation of the right to a post-verdict hearing (e.g., via motions in limine or other district-court practice) is sufficient procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity and longstanding nature of ensnarement weigh against Supreme Court review
rubrics_metrics.description: The ensnarement defense is longstanding and uncontroversial in patent law; courts have applied it sparingly and consistently for decades. Empirical claims: since 1988 the Federal Circuit mentioned ensnarement and the doctrine of equivalents in only 23 decisions; district courts mentioned them in 112 orders since 1993; doctrine of equivalents mentioned in a small percentage of patent cases, indicating the issue is not recurring enough to warrant certiorari.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether an issue merits certiorari, consider whether the doctrine is novel, controversial, or recurring nationally; infrequent, settled doctrines are poor candidates for Supreme Court review.
